title: The birds who fed a guest
hookLine: a king asks who is greater, the monk or the householder; a family of birds answers
carry: grihastha: the householder's life is a path too
tomorrow: a proud monk burns two birds with a look. who humbles him?

cards: Who is greater: the one who stays in the world, or the one who leaves it? The householder with a family and a mortgage, or the monk with a bowl and a road? It's an old argument.
Vivekananda's New York talks kept circling back to work: his listeners' jobs, their families, their duties. In the second chapter of Karma-Yoga he takes the argument on directly. Not with a ruling.
With a story about a king, a monk who said no, and a family of birds.

teach.h: WHO IS GREATER: HOUSEHOLDER OR MONK?
teach.b: A king asked every monk who came to his court the same question: which is greater, the householder or the monk?
One day a young monk said: each is great in its own place. Come, and I'll show you. In a neighboring kingdom a princess was choosing her husband before the whole court.
She chose a young monk. He said no, and walked out into the forest. The king followed, lost his way, and night fell.
Cold and lost, he lay down under a tree.

teach.h: THE BIRDS WHO FED A GUEST.
teach.b: In that tree lived a family of small birds. The father bird looked down and said: there is a guest in our house, and he's cold. He flew off and came back with a burning twig in his beak, and a fire was made.
Then: our guest must be hungry, and we have nothing to give. And he dropped into the fire. His mate followed.
Then their little ones. The lesson: the young man who turned down a kingdom was great as a monk. These birds were great as householders.
Each is great in its own place, the chapter's title.
Hindu tradition has a name for the birds' stage of life: grihastha, the householder.

teach.h: EACH IS GREAT IN ITS OWN PLACE.
teach.b: It's honored as the stage that feeds all the others, students, elders, monks and guests. The path isn't only for people who leave.
And the Taittiriya Upanishad, in its parting words to students, says: let the guest be a god to you. The birds took it all the way.

how: In the Ramakrishna and Vedanta movements, Vivekananda's Karma Yoga is read as a guide to treating ordinary work and family duty as spiritual practice, and hospitality to guests is honored in Hindu homes as a sacred duty.

o: someone living in the world, with family and work
the eldest man, who heads the family's home
someone who owns a house and the land under it

games.q: the story and its lesson — tap the pairs.

s: Vivekananda taught that only monks can walk the path of karma yoga
his lecture argues each is great in its own place: householder and monk alike.
in the story, the birds give their lives for a guest
the father, then his mate, then their little ones drop into the fire to feed their guest.
Karma Yoga began as a book Vivekananda wrote in India
it grew from talks he gave in New York.

games.q: a king asks you: who is greater, the monk who leaves the world, or the householder who stays?
o: the monk: he gave up the most.
each is great in its own place: both can be the path.
the householder: monks don't do real work.
games.why: the young monk who refused a kingdom, and the birds who fed a guest: each great in its own place. the grihastha's life is a path too.

practice: Let your own place come to mind, the real one: the desk, the counter, the people who need something from you this week. Breathe in and see one piece of work that's yours to do; breathe out and let it be enough of a place.
If you pray, offer that one task quietly, the way the birds offered their fire; if you don't, just hold it, whole and ordinary, and rest.

wordCard.voice: Householder, in Sanskrit grihastha: one who lives in the world with a family and work. The householder and the monk can both walk the path, each great in its own place.

orig.note: Sanskrit: karma, action (from kṛ, to do) + yoga, a yoking or discipline: action as a path.

carryVoice: Your line: grihastha: the householder's life is a path too. The birds fed their guest with everything. That's day two hundred sixty-two.

sources.ref: Swami Vivekananda, Karma Yoga (1896), ch. 2, 'Each Is Great in His Own Place' (the king, the young monk and the birds)
Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.2 (atithi devo bhava: let the guest be as a god)
Manusmriti 3.77–78 (the householder supports the other stages of life)
